indicators.note: Something done awkwardly comes out clumsily rearranged, so the letters before it are not left in the order they were given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A client making clumsy romantic advances at the person serving him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Courts' is a verb in the picture and a bag of letters in the wordplay. Short anagrams whose fodder is two ordinary words are hard to spot because the sentence reads so naturally.
explanation.definitionFit: A customer is the person buying from a shop or firm, which is what 'client' names in a professional practice — the same relationship, a different counter.

parts.note: a bobby is a British policeman, named after Sir Robert Peel, and the possessive s comes across with him
a hop is a dance, the village-hall sort

explanation.surface: Nick turning up at a dance with Bobby.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick and Bobby read as two lads at a dance, and both are police words: the nick is the station, a bobby is the constable who takes you there.
explanation.definitionFit: The nick is British slang for the police station, and a cop shop is that same building in the same offhand register.

clue.text: Woman avoids US anarchy to an extent

indicators.note: Something true only to an extent is true in part, so only part of the words before it is taken — an unbroken run of their letters.

parts.note: an unbroken run that starts on the last letter of 'avoids', takes 'US' whole and stops two letters into 'anarchy'

explanation.surface: A woman steering clear of chaos in the States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'US anarchy' reads as a remark about American politics, and that is where the eye stays while the letters slide past underneath. A hidden run that starts on the last letter of a word is the hardest kind to see.
explanation.definitionFit: Susan is an ordinary English given name, so 'Woman' is the only category label a setter can hang on it.

clue.text: Ninth bloke taken ill, not working

indicators.note: Someone taken ill is no longer in good order, and letters taken ill come out of the clue in a different arrangement.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: The ninth man in a queue being carried off sick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ninth bloke' is a phrase nobody says, and that oddity is the tell — wording that would never occur in speech is usually there for its letters. The definition covers a man off sick and a machine broken alike.
explanation.definitionFit: A boiler or a kettle on the blink has stopped working properly, the everyday British phrase for a gadget that has failed.

definitions.meaning: read as the verb on a travel site, and meant as one named book of the Bible
read as the flight being booked, and meant as a mass leaving

explanation.surface: A terse instruction to reserve a seat on an outbound flight.
explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions abutting, which is why the clue is only two words long. 'Book' wants to be the verb you do on a travel site and is the noun instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Exodus is the second book of the Bible, named for the event that is also the word's other sense: a mass departure from Egypt.

indicators.note: What is set about a thing is wrapped round it, so the word named first closes round the letter that follows.

parts.note: a wrong is a sin
p is the coin, a penny, as printed on British prices

explanation.surface: Being mistaken about the short outing Penny made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrong about' reads as one phrase — a person who has got something wrong — and splits into a word and an instruction. The capital letter sells Penny as a woman when she is small change.
explanation.definitionFit: A spin is a short pleasure drive, as in taking the car out for a spin, so 'little trip' is the outing rather than the stumble.

parts.note: pro means in favour of, as in pro-European
a test is an experiment

explanation.surface: Crowds marching in support of an experiment.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as one news sentence, and the two pieces of the answer are the very words that make the sentence work. 'Demonstration' is the march rather than the laboratory display.
explanation.definitionFit: A protest is a public demonstration — placards, a route, a rally — rather than a formal objection lodged on paper.

indicators.note: In a down clue, what comes from the south is travelling upwards, so its letters are read bottom to top.

parts.note: to attack is to set on someone, and SET ON climbing the grid spells these letters

explanation.surface: A commander watching an assault come in from the southern flank.
explanation.walkthrough: The military picture is complete without a word of it being wordplay, which is the point: 'from the south' is an order about direction on the page, not the line of the attack. 'Set on' is the old phrase for launching at someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To note something is to observe it — he noted the time — so the answer matches 'Observes' as a present-tense verb.

definitions.meaning: read as being on your feet, and meant as the rank or status someone holds
read as the spot in which to stand, and meant on its own as a location

explanation.surface: Somewhere to stand, as on a football terrace.
explanation.walkthrough: Two very common nouns side by side give a solver almost nothing to grip. The trap is reading them together as standing room when each is a separate definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's position is their standing in a firm or a society, and a position is also the place a thing occupies — status and location, the same noun twice.

indicators.note: What is in a thing sits within it, so the letter named first is written inside the word that follows.

parts.note: a cot is a bed
l is the usual short form of left

explanation.surface: A pistol left lying in the bed.
explanation.walkthrough: A gun in the bed is a whole thriller in four words, and every one of them is doing crossword duty instead. 'Left' is the single letter, not the past tense of leave.
explanation.definitionFit: Colt is the American maker whose revolvers were so common that the name became the gun, so 'Gun' is a definition by example.

clue.text: The box of novelties I cooked up

indicators.note: Something cooked up has been knocked together out of whatever was to hand, so the letters go into the pot and come out in a new order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A box of gimmicks someone has invented.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooked up' reads as inventing a story, which is exactly what a box of novelties would be. The definition is two words because it is a nickname rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: The box is the long-standing British nickname for the television set, from the days when it was a wooden box in the corner of the room.

clue.text: Glaswegian woman joining church for this reason

indicators.note: Joining puts one thing next to another, so the two pieces are written end to end in the order the clue gives them.

parts.note: hen is what a Glaswegian calls a woman, the Scottish equivalent of 'love' or 'pet'
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A Glasgow woman going along to church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hen' is Glasgow's everyday address for a woman, the way 'pal' works for a man, and it is the piece a solver outside Scotland is least likely to have. The church is the established one, CE.
explanation.definitionFit: Hence means for this reason — 'hence the delay' — the formal connective that introduces a consequence.

clue.text: Futile advice on how to cut gas bill?

definitions.text: Futile advice on how to cut gas bill?

parts.note: read as a tip that will do nobody any good, and meant as the plain adjective on its own
meant as the advice itself, the answer broken into two words: burn less of it

explanation.surface: Someone dismissing a tip for lowering the heating bill.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer has to be read twice, once as the adjective the first word defines and once split in two as the tip being given. Energy-saving advice really does come down to those two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Useless means futile, of no use at all, and the same seven letters divided differently spell the only sure way to cut a gas bill.

parts.note: port is the fortified drink

indicators.note: A case is the shell a thing sits in, so only the outside letters of the word that follows are taken.

parts.note: the outer letters of landlady

explanation.surface: Working through a case of the landlady's stout in the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stout' is the black beer in the picture and the definition wants the body shape instead. Two drinks in one clue is the whole disguise, and only one of them supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Portly describes a stout, comfortably heavy figure, usually a man's, so 'stout' is the adjective for a build rather than the pint.

parts.note: to rat is to desert your side, as rats leave a sinking ship
a race is a people

explanation.surface: People in the desert fighting to stay alive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Desert' looks like sand and is the verb to abandon, with the stress on the second syllable. A rat deserts and a race is a people: two dictionary senses nobody reaches for first.
explanation.definitionFit: The rat race is the daily scramble to keep a living going, which is what 'struggle to survive' becomes once it is office life rather than the wild.

indicators.note: One road crossing another cuts through its middle, so these letters go inside the word just named.

parts.note: a peer is a nobleman, a lord of the realm
st is the address abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: A lord being bothered while he crosses the road.
explanation.walkthrough: The insertion splits the nobleman between his two Es, which is where clues like this get hard: the container opens in the middle rather than at an obvious seam.
explanation.definitionFit: To pester someone is to annoy them by not letting up, the repeated nagging sense rather than a single irritation.

clue.text: Give new name to island in muddled letter

indicators.note: What is muddled has been put out of its proper order, so these letters are to be rearranged.

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters
i is the map abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: Renaming an island mentioned in a garbled letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter' is correspondence in the picture and a six-letter word to shuffle in fact, with the island's single letter thrown in alongside. Anagrams that swallow an extra letter are the easiest ones to miscount.
explanation.definitionFit: To retitle something is to give it a new name — a film retitled for its American release — so the definition is the phrase spelt out.

clue.text: Gather a ship's complement in the auditorium

indicators.note: An auditorium is the part of a theatre where people go to listen, so what matters is how the words before it sound when said aloud.

parts.note: a ship's complement is the crew it carries, and 'a crew' spoken aloud spells this instead

explanation.surface: Assembling a ship's whole crew in a theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complement' is the naval word for the full body of hands a vessel carries, spelt with an E and nothing to do with praise. The auditorium is the listening instruction, not the room the sailors fill.
explanation.definitionFit: Interest accrues by gathering steadily — evidence accrues, leave accrues — so 'Gather' is the piling-up sense of the verb.

parts.note: read as any picture at the cinema, and meant as one particular blockbuster
read as flopping with audiences, and meant of the liner the film is named for, which sank on her maiden voyage

explanation.surface: A film that bombed with the critics and the public.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went down' is what a picture does with an audience and what a ship does in the North Atlantic. James Cameron's 1997 film was the biggest hit of its day, so the only thing that went down was the liner.
explanation.definitionFit: Titanic is the film named for the White Star liner that struck an iceberg in 1912, so the disaster in the clue is the ship's rather than the box office's.

indicators.note: A man aboard is inside the vessel, so the letters named first go within the word that follows.

parts.note: also means too
AB is an able seaman, the navy's rating for an ordinary sailor

explanation.surface: A sailor on board who has been banned as well.
explanation.walkthrough: AB is the commonest sailor in crosswords and worth learning on sight. 'Aboard' does double duty, painting the deck and saying that the letters go inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Something taboo is banned by custom rather than by law — a subject nobody may raise — so 'banned' is the plain sense of the adjective.

clue.text: Popular place to rent in bay

parts.note: what is popular is in, the way a colour is in this season
a let is a place rented out, from the 'to let' board outside it

explanation.surface: A sought-after holiday flat to rent on a bay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Popular place to rent' is one estate agent's phrase in the picture and two separate pieces in the wordplay, and the seam between them is what the clue hides.
explanation.definitionFit: An inlet is a small bay, the narrow arm of sea that cuts into a coastline.

parts.note: a lass is a girl, northern English and Scots
Oscar is O in the radio alphabet

explanation.surface: A girl photographed with an Academy Award.
explanation.walkthrough: Oscar belongs to the radio alphabet that also gives Charlie and Tango, and the statuette is the disguise. 'Catch' is a verb, which is how you know the answer has to be one.
explanation.definitionFit: To lasso a steer is to catch it with a thrown loop of rope, so 'Catch' is the verb the cowboy's rope performs.

indicators.note: Whatever is trapped in a place cannot get out of it, so the answer is sitting inside the word that follows.

parts.note: held inside cupBOARd

explanation.surface: An animal shut in a kitchen cupboard.
explanation.walkthrough: A hidden word buried in one long word has no join between words to catch the eye, which is what makes a four-letter run this short so easy to walk past.
explanation.definitionFit: A boar is the tusked wild pig of European forests, the undomesticated ancestor of the farm pig.

clue.text: Coach arranged something for children to play with

definitions.text: something for children to play with

parts.note: to coach someone is to train them
things arranged in place have been set there

explanation.surface: A sports coach laying on an activity to keep the children amused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arranged' sits exactly where an anagram indicator would sit and is a synonym instead, which is the one real trap here. 'Coach' is the verb to train rather than the bus or the man with the whistle.
explanation.definitionFit: A train set is the toy railway of track and engines a child lays out on the floor, so the definition names it by what it is for.

parts.note: o is the standard short form of old
men is the army's own word for soldiers, as in officers and men

explanation.surface: A warning passed down by old soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is smooth enough that 'old soldiers' reads as a single phrase, while the wordplay splits it and takes one letter from the first half.
explanation.definitionFit: An omen is a sign of what is coming, and a bad omen is a warning — the noun sense, matching the noun in the clue.

clue.text: Supporter of runner, perhaps — someone very tall and thin?

indicators.note: Perhaps marks the word before it as only one instance of something, so what is wanted is the general word it is an example of.

parts.note: a runner is one kind of bean, the climbing sort grown up canes
a pole is what supports a climbing plant

explanation.surface: A fan backing an athlete who is built like a stick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runner' is the bean of the vegetable patch, not the athlete the surface puts on the track, and the supporter is the cane pushed in beside it. Both halves of the clue end up describing the same garden object.
explanation.definitionFit: A beanpole is what the British call a very tall thin person, borrowing the name of the thin cane that props up bean plants.
